details.definition: A language concurrency memory model specifies which writes a shared-memory read may observe.
details.motivation: Define permitted concurrent behavior while allowing implementation optimizations.
details.origin: Semantic foundation: program actions and ordering relations. This is a language contract, not an address-translation mechanism.
details.first_principles: Synchronization contributes to happens-before ordering. Correctly synchronized, data-race-free programs receive the sequential-consistency guarantees stated by their language.
details.does: Constrains legal executions and transformations of shared-memory programs.
details.outcome: Rules for reasoning about visibility and ordering across concurrent execution.
details.useWhen: Sharing mutable state across Java threads or Go goroutines; apply each language's precise rules.

empowered_by.how: Defines the ordering contributed by synchronization operations.

verification.scope: Shared-memory concurrency semantics, illustrated by Java SE 25 and Go; not allocation, ownership or virtual memory.

details.definition: A database management system manages stored data and operations over it. PostgreSQL and SQLite are SQL database engines with transaction support.
details.motivation: Applications need to query and update structured data through an engine rather than implement every storage operation themselves.
details.origin: The relational branch traces to Ted Codd's 1970 relational model; databases also existed in earlier hierarchical and network forms.
details.first_principles: Separate the data interface from the engine's physical implementation.
details.does: Exposes data definition, queries and transactional updates. The interface does not require one universal index structure.
details.outcome: Reusable data management; physical design and engine selection still affect performance.
details.useWhen: When application data needs structured queries and transactional updates.

empowered_by.how: Groups database changes into commit or rollback units.
empowered_by.forCase: Transactional SQL engines such as PostgreSQL and SQLite.

verification.scope: Introductory SQL DBMS example; not every database model or engine.
verification.furtherResearch: Storage-engine internals, non-relational models and workload-specific operating costs.

details.definition: The relational model represents a database as relations: sets of tuples whose attributes draw values from defined domains. A table is a common presentation of a relation, but physical row order and access paths are not part of the logical model.
details.motivation: Codd proposed the model so application programs and users could work with data without depending on its machine-level representation, stored ordering, or navigation links.
details.origin: Edgar F. Codd published “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks” in Communications of the ACM in June 1970. IBM later built System R to test whether the model could support a practical, high-performance database system.
details.first_principles: Describe data by values, domains, tuples, relations, and integrity rules; derive results with operations over relations; keep that logical description separate from indexes, record placement, and other physical choices.
details.does: Gives a DBMS a logical structure for defining relations and deriving new result relations through operations such as selection, projection, and joins. Normalization can reduce certain redundancy and update anomalies, but schema design still requires judgment.
details.outcome: Queries can express required results while the DBMS chooses physical access paths. Applications gain data independence, although schema changes and performance characteristics can still affect them.
details.useWhen: Use it when data fits typed, related records and the system benefits from declarative queries and integrity constraints. Other models may fit graph traversal, unstructured documents, or specialized access patterns better.

empowers.how: Provides the relation-oriented data model that SQL implementations query and update.
empowers.forCase: Relational operations implemented by SQL database systems.

empowered_by.how: Relations are sets of tuples over domains, and relational query formalisms express predicates over them.
empowered_by.forCase: The formal relational model; SQL adds features and differs in details.

traceDown: DBMS selects physical operators and access paths

verification.scope: Core relational model, data-independence motivation, and the documented Codd/System R lineage; not every normal form, relational language, or database workload.

claims.agreement: Codd's paper defines the model and its data-independence goal; IBM's history independently describes the same model, motivation, 1970 publication, and System R lineage.
PostgreSQL's model descriptions and MIT's lecture agree on relations, attributes, tuples, relational operations, and the separation between relation-oriented use and database mechanisms.

verification.furtherResearch: Candidate keys, nulls, integrity theory, normal forms beyond the introductory account, relational completeness, and differences between the mathematical model and SQL bags/null semantics.

details.definition: SQL is a standardized database language family used to define, query, and modify data and to control transactions and other database objects. Concrete systems implement SQL dialects rather than one perfectly identical language.
details.motivation: SQL lets a user state which data result or change is required while the database system chooses much of the execution procedure and physical access path.
details.origin: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce presented SEQUEL at SIGFIDET in 1974 for querying an integrated relational database. The work became SQL through IBM's System R project; later ANSI and ISO standards established portable language specifications.
details.first_principles: A statement describes a result set or state change over named tables and expressions. Parsing, semantic analysis, planning, execution, transaction handling, and storage are separate downstream responsibilities.
details.does: Defines schemas with statements such as CREATE TABLE; reads data with SELECT; changes it with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE; and delimits transactional work with commands such as BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK. Exact syntax and behavior depend on the implementation and standard version.
details.outcome: Applications can express complex data operations compactly and let the DBMS optimize their execution. Portability is substantial but incomplete because implementations expose extensions, omissions, and behavioral differences.
details.useWhen: Use SQL for relational data definition, querying, reporting, integrity rules, and transactional changes. Confirm the target engine's documentation for dialect, isolation, type, and null behavior.

empowers.how: Provides the language interface through which applications define, retrieve, aggregate, and update relational data.

empowered_by.how: Supplies the tabular relations and declarative operations that SQL adapts into a practical database language.
empowered_by.forCase: The relational core of SQL; SQL also contains features outside pure relational algebra.

traceDown: SQL text from an application or user
Indexes, pages, logs, and persistent bytes

verification.scope: SQL's core data-definition, query, modification, and transaction role plus documented SEQUEL/System R lineage; not the full current ISO grammar or every vendor dialect.

claims.agreement: The PostgreSQL and SQLite language references document SQL's schema, query, modification, and transaction roles; the original SEQUEL paper establishes the declarative relational intent.
The 1974 IBM paper and Computer History Museum's SQL reunion record Chamberlin and Boyce's SEQUEL work and its transition into SQL/System R.
Both sources show that concrete SQL implementations have documented conformance boundaries and dialect-specific behavior.

verification.furtherResearch: Formal ISO editions, bag and null semantics, recursive SQL, procedural extensions, security statements, and exact portability differences among engines.

lectures.title: CMU 15-445: Modern SQL
lectures.role: Course schedule links the SQL lecture, notes, and video; factual verification uses the paired written sources.

details.definition: A database transaction groups operations into a unit that commits or rolls back. Transaction systems coordinate visibility between concurrent work and use recovery mechanisms so acknowledged changes satisfy the database's durability guarantees.
details.motivation: A multi-step change can otherwise leave partial results after an error, expose inconsistent intermediate state to concurrent work, or disappear after a crash.
details.origin: Transaction processing predates SQL. A documented relational-database milestone is IBM System R: its 1976 architecture described triggered transactions, logging, recovery, and consistency for shared updates. This is a lineage claim, not a first-invention claim.
details.first_principles: Atomicity treats a unit as all-or-nothing; consistency depends on transactions and declared/application invariants; isolation constrains observations of concurrent work; durability governs committed results. Implementations realize these properties with mechanisms such as concurrency control, logging, and recovery.
details.does: BEGIN establishes an explicit transaction context; COMMIT requests that its effects become durable and visible according to the engine's rules; ROLLBACK abandons its effects. Isolation levels trade stronger guarantees against possible blocking, aborts, or anomalies.
details.outcome: Applications can compose related database changes without manually exposing every recovery and concurrency mechanism. They must still choose transaction boundaries, handle failures or retries, and preserve business invariants.
details.useWhen: Use a transaction when operations must succeed as a unit or must observe a defined concurrency guarantee, such as transferring value or updating related records. Keep transactions appropriately bounded and select isolation from the anomaly requirements.

empowers.how: Turns several reads and writes into a controlled commit-or-rollback unit with defined concurrent visibility.
empowers.forCase: Database operations whose partial completion or concurrency anomalies would violate requirements.

empowered_by.how: Coordination orders or separates conflicting work, while logging and recovery connect commit decisions to persistent state.
empowered_by.forCase: Representative DBMS implementations; exact algorithms vary.

traceDown: SQL statements read or stage changes
Concurrency control manages conflicts and visibility

verification.scope: Local database transaction boundaries, ACID responsibilities, concurrency visibility, and a System R lineage milestone; not distributed commit or every engine's recovery algorithm.

claims.agreement: Both engine manuals define transaction boundaries and commit/rollback behavior; PostgreSQL also states atomicity, visibility, and durable-recording goals, while SQLite documents its concurrency limits.
PostgreSQL and MIT course materials agree that concurrency control supplies isolation and that logging/recovery supports atomicity and durability.
The contemporary System R architecture and IBM researchers' later history document transaction, logging, recovery, and shared-update work in the System R project.

verification.furtherResearch: Write-ahead logging details, serializability theory, deadlocks, optimistic control, MVCC variants, savepoints, distributed transactions, sagas, and engine-specific failure guarantees.

lectures.title: MIT 6.830: Transactions
lectures.role: Lecture notes covering ACID and serializability.

details.definition: A database index is an additional access structure for locating rows by selected values.
details.motivation: Avoid examining every row for a selective lookup.
details.origin: One important lineage is the B-tree, invented by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight. This is the origin of that index family, not of every database indexing technique.
details.first_principles: An index orders or organizes keys so an access method can narrow the search.
details.does: CREATE INDEX builds an access path. The planner chooses whether to use it; having an index does not force its use.
details.outcome: Faster applicable lookups, with storage and update-maintenance overhead.
details.useWhen: Repeated selective predicates justify maintaining an extra structure. Inspect the actual plan rather than assuming every index helps.

empowered_by.how: Organizes indexed keys for the selected access method.

verification.scope: Mechanism and use verified; historical priority remains unverified.

claims.agreement: Both engines document index creation and lookup paths; PostgreSQL explicitly documents maintenance overhead.

verification.furtherResearch: Index maintenance costs need a second explicit source; other access-method histories need separate evidence.

details.definition: Query processing turns a declarative request into an executable plan and produces its result.
details.motivation: The same requested result can have execution paths with very different costs.
details.origin: A documented milestone is Selinger and colleagues' 1979 System R paper on access-path selection. It describes choosing execution paths for declarative SQL, not the invention of every query-processing technique.
details.first_principles: Choose among valid scans and other operators using estimates of their work.
details.does: The engine can use a table scan or an applicable index; additional operations perform required sorting and joins.
details.outcome: Applications state a query while the engine selects execution details. Estimates can be imperfect, so a chosen plan need not be optimal.
details.useWhen: For SQL execution and diagnosing query performance; inspect the engine's plan output.

empowered_by.how: The planner may select an index scan instead of a table scan.
empowered_by.forCase: Queries with a useful available index; not a universal dependency.

verification.scope: Introductory query processing and a documented System R milestone.
verification.furtherResearch: Join algorithms, cardinality estimation and subsequent optimizer designs.

details.definition: Virtual memory gives a process an address space whose addresses are translated to physical memory.
details.motivation: Run programs in isolated address spaces while sharing physical memory.
details.origin: Manchester's Atlas, operational in 1962, pioneered virtual memory through its single-level store. This is a documented milestone, not a claim that every modern VM technique originated there.
details.first_principles: With paging, a virtual page number selects a physical frame; the offset within the page is preserved. Translation also checks access permissions.
details.does: The kernel installs page-table mappings. Hardware uses them for address translation; a TLB caches translations to avoid repeated page-table reads.
details.outcome: Independent address spaces and protected mappings, at the cost of page-table storage and translation misses. A TLB miss requires translation work; it is not necessarily a page fault.
details.useWhen: When an OS must isolate programs and map their virtual addresses onto shared physical memory.

empowered_by.how: Page-table entries map virtual pages to physical frames and carry access permissions.
Caches translations; a miss falls back to page-table lookup.

traceDown: Permission check and physical frame plus offset

verification.scope: Introductory paged virtual memory; implementation details vary by architecture.

claims.agreement: OSTEP paging/TLB chapters and xv6 chapter 3 agree on mappings, permissions, translation caching and lookup costs.
Both identify Manchester Atlas in 1962 as a virtual-memory milestone.

verification.furtherResearch: Does not cover nested virtualization, NUMA policy, page replacement or architecture-specific TLB invalidation.

details.definition: TCP supplies an ordered, reliable byte stream; UDP supplies datagrams without guaranteed delivery or ordering.
details.motivation: Applications need transport between endpoints above IP, with different choices about reliability and message boundaries.
details.origin: The Internet protocol specifications define TCP and UDP separately. RFC 9293 is the consolidated TCP specification; RFC 768 defines UDP. Linux documents implementations of both.
details.first_principles: TCP tracks sequence numbers and retransmits lost data. UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not add TCP's stream recovery.
details.does: Port numbers distinguish application endpoints. TCP transmits its segments over IP; UDP transmits datagrams over IP.
details.outcome: TCP handles loss recovery but applications must delimit messages in its byte stream. UDP applications must tolerate loss or add the required recovery.
details.useWhen: Choose TCP for an ordered byte stream. Choose UDP when the application needs datagrams and handles the consequences of unreliable delivery.

empowered_by.how: Carries transport headers and payload between addressed hosts.

verification.scope: Transport service and IP dependency; Linux documentation corroborates the RFCs.

claims.agreement: TCP claims are paired between RFC 9293 and tcp(7); UDP claims between RFC 768 and udp(7).

verification.furtherResearch: Congestion algorithms, application framing, QUIC and failure detection need separate treatment.

details.definition: Working storage for an operating computer; this entry follows the common DRAM implementation.
details.motivation: Provide dense, addressable storage for active computation.
details.origin: Robert Dennard conceived one-transistor DRAM in 1966; his patent was issued in 1968. Earlier main-memory technologies predate DRAM.
details.first_principles: A DRAM cell stores a bit as capacitor charge and uses a transistor for access.
details.does: Memory circuitry reads and writes cells and refreshes their stored charge.
details.outcome: Dense working storage that needs power and refresh; it is not persistent storage.
details.useWhen: Keeping active data in a DRAM-based system.

empowered_by.how: Stores bits in transistor-capacitor cells.

verification.scope: DRAM implementation, not all main-memory technologies.

claims.agreement: IBM's history and Dennard's own account agree on conception in 1966 and patent issuance in 1968.

verification.furtherResearch: Memory-controller scheduling, ECC, refresh timing and non-DRAM implementations.

lectures.role: Lecture with an available MIT transcript.

details.definition: For binary logic design, Boolean algebra describes values 0 and 1 using AND, OR and NOT.
details.motivation: Express and simplify a circuit's required logical behavior before choosing gates.
details.origin: Conceptual foundation: two-valued logic and algebraic identities. This entry does not yet establish historical priority.
details.first_principles: Equivalent expressions give identical outputs for every input combination. OR is not ordinary integer addition: 1 OR 1 = 1.
details.does: Rewrites expressions using identities such as A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C).
details.outcome: A logically equivalent expression that can be mapped to a circuit.
details.useWhen: Specifying or simplifying binary combinational functions.
details.empowers: Truth-table reasoning and combinational logic synthesis.

empowered_by.how: Defines truth values and operations used in circuit equations.

verification.scope: Binary switching algebra; historical origin remains unverified.
verification.furtherResearch: Verify Boole's original development and the later application to switching with two sources.

details.definition: A logic gate implements a Boolean function on digital signals; a two-input AND gate outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.
details.motivation: Provide reusable building blocks for larger digital functions.
details.origin: Implementation chain: Boolean function to switching circuit. CMOS uses transistor networks; logic gates are not limited to CMOS.
details.first_principles: A truth table specifies logical behavior. Physical gates also have propagation delays and electrical operating limits.
details.does: Produces the specified output after inputs settle within the device's timing and electrical requirements.
details.outcome: A digital output usable by subsequent circuitry.
details.useWhen: Implementing Boolean decisions in hardware, within the selected device's data-sheet limits.
details.empowers: Combinational functions built by interconnecting gates.

empowered_by.how: Controls conductive paths to implement a gate's truth table.

verification.scope: Gate behavior and a CMOS implementation chain; no first-inventor claim.

details.definition: A combinational circuit's settled outputs depend on its current inputs, without stored input history.
details.motivation: Implement a specified input-to-output function in hardware.
details.origin: Construction chain: truth table or Boolean equations, then interconnected logic gates.
details.first_principles: The same valid input combination gives the same settled output; a truth table enumerates all combinations.
details.does: Combines gate functions to compute the required result.
details.outcome: A hardware implementation of the specified Boolean function.
details.useWhen: Computing functions that require no retained state.
details.empowers: The computation portion of sequential systems.

empowered_by.how: Interconnects Boolean operators to implement the function.

verification.scope: Combinational functional model and construction chain; historical priority is not asserted.

details.definition: Sequential circuits retain state, allowing behavior to depend on previous inputs.
details.motivation: Remember information needed for a later operation.
details.origin: Construction chain: state storage combined with logic that computes the next state.
details.first_principles: Current state and inputs determine the next state. In a synchronous implementation, clocked storage captures it at the designated clock edge.
details.does: Repeatedly computes and stores a new state.
details.outcome: A circuit with behavior across successive steps.
details.useWhen: Implementing stateful digital control.

empowered_by.how: Computes the next state from current state and inputs.
Retains the encoded state between clock edges.

verification.scope: Stateful circuit model and synchronous construction, not all asynchronous designs or historical priority.

details.definition: An edge-triggered D flip-flop stores one bit by sampling D at a designated clock edge.
details.motivation: Keep state stable between clock events.
details.origin: Construction example: oppositely controlled master and slave latches form an edge-triggered storage element.
details.first_principles: D must meet setup and hold requirements around the sampling edge. Q changes after a clock-to-output delay, not instantaneously.
details.does: Captures D and retains the sampled value until another active edge, except when an implemented asynchronous control overrides it.
details.outcome: One retained state bit.
details.useWhen: Building clocked state storage; use the particular device's timing specifications.

empowered_by.uses: Gates with feedback and latch control
empowered_by.how: Retains a bit using feedback; master/slave control provides edge-triggered behavior.

verification.scope: D flip-flop function, timing and master/slave construction; no historical priority claim.
verification.furtherResearch: Historical origin and other flip-flop families remain outside this treatment.

details.definition: A counter is a sequential circuit that advances through a prescribed sequence of states.
details.motivation: Retain a count across input events.
details.origin: Construction chain: stored count bits plus logic for the next count. Synchronous counters share a clock; ripple counters clock later stages from earlier stages.
details.first_principles: An n-bit binary up-counter increments modulo 2^n. Its finite width therefore wraps after the largest value unless additional control changes the sequence.
details.does: In a synchronous design, computes the next count and captures it on an enabled clock edge.
details.outcome: A binary representation of progress through the counting sequence.
details.useWhen: Counting qualified clock events or implementing a bounded sequence.

empowered_by.how: Stores count bits while combinational logic selects their next values.

verification.scope: Binary synchronous counter mechanism and comparison with ripple construction; no historical priority claim.

details.definition: An adder computes binary addition. An arithmetic and logic unit selects among supported arithmetic and logical operations on operands.
details.origin: Construction chain: Boolean logic implements sum and carry; arithmetic and logic blocks plus result selection form an ALU.
details.first_principles: A full adder consumes two operand bits and a carry-in, producing a sum bit and carry-out. Multi-bit carry handling affects delay.
details.does: Computes candidate operations and selects the requested result in the illustrated combinational ALU design.
details.outcome: An operation result for the surrounding datapath.
details.useWhen: Implementing processor arithmetic and logical instructions; supported operations depend on the design.
details.empowers: Instruction execution in a processor datapath.

empowered_by.how: Combines sum/carry logic, Boolean operations and multiplexers.
empowered_by.forCase: The teaching ALU designs cited here.

traceDown: Arithmetic or logic block and result selection

verification.scope: Binary adders and teaching ALU construction; no universal ALU instruction set or historical priority claim.

details.definition: A finite-state machine models behavior using a finite set of states and input-dependent transitions.
details.motivation: Make a controller's dependence on past events explicit.
details.origin: Construction chain: describe transitions, encode states as bits, implement next-state logic and state storage.
details.first_principles: For a fully specified deterministic machine, each state/input combination selects one next state.
details.does: Uses the current state and input to compute the next state, then updates the stored state.
details.outcome: A reproducible sequence of state transitions for a given initial state and input sequence.
details.useWhen: Designing finite digital controllers.
details.empowers: A hardware implementation through state registers and combinational logic.

empowered_by.how: Encodes the finite state in stored bits and computes transitions with logic.
empowered_by.forCase: Clocked hardware implementation, not the abstract mathematical definition.

verification.scope: Deterministic finite controller and hardware realization; no historical priority claim.

details.definition: Circuits that store and retrieve bits; the concrete example here is a one-transistor DRAM cell.
details.motivation: Represent a stored bit using a compact physical cell.
details.origin: Dennard's one-transistor DRAM design was conceived in 1966 and patented in 1968.
details.first_principles: Capacitor charge encodes the bit; a transistor controls access.
details.does: Read/write circuitry accesses cells; refresh restores leaking charge.
details.outcome: Compact storage requires refresh and power to retain data.
details.useWhen: Implementing DRAM storage.

empowered_by.how: Controls access to the storage capacitor.

verification.scope: One-transistor DRAM only; SRAM and nonvolatile cells need their own entries.
verification.furtherResearch: SRAM, ROM, flash, sense amplifiers and timing specifications.

details.definition: Voltage describes electric potential difference; current describes the rate of charge flow.
details.motivation: Describe electrical behavior quantitatively when analyzing a circuit.
details.origin: Physical foundation: charge, energy and electromagnetic interaction. These are physical quantities, not inventions with a single software-style author.
details.first_principles: Current is charge per unit time. Circuit models relate currents and voltages through element laws and conservation constraints.
details.does: For an ideal resistor, V = I R relates voltage, current and resistance. It is a component model, not the universal behavior of every device.
details.outcome: A tractable circuit model whose predictions depend on the element models and their applicability.
details.useWhen: Analyzing how electronic components respond to applied electrical signals.

empowered_by.how: Moving charge supplies current; potential difference describes electrical energy per charge.
empowered_by.forCase: Physical electrical circuits. This is the museum's physical boundary, not a dependency on another software abstraction.

verification.scope: Introductory circuit quantities and resistor model.
verification.furtherResearch: Field equations, distributed circuits and nonlinear device models.

details.definition: The physics of charge carriers and energy bands in materials whose conductivity can be engineered.
details.motivation: Explain and control conduction instead of treating a semiconductor as a fixed resistor.
details.origin: Conceptual foundation: solid-state energy bands and electron/hole transport. No single inventor of this branch of physics is asserted.
details.first_principles: Thermal excitation and dopants change carrier populations. Donors support n-type material; acceptors support p-type material.
details.does: Relates composition and excitation to electron and hole concentrations and electrical behavior.
details.outcome: Controlled electrical properties; behavior depends on temperature and doping rather than a universal on/off rule.
details.useWhen: Explaining the semiconductor regions inside diodes and transistors.

empowered_by.how: Carrier motion constitutes electrical current.
empowered_by.forCase: Electron and hole conduction in semiconductor devices.

verification.scope: Introductory carrier and doping model; conceptual lineage, not a historical priority claim.
verification.furtherResearch: Band-structure derivation, carrier mobility, recombination and device-specific transport.

details.definition: Silicon, element Si with atomic number 14, is a semiconductor used in microelectronic devices.
details.motivation: Provide material whose electrical behavior can be controlled through preparation and doping.
details.origin: Berzelius isolated silicon in 1824. Elemental silicon is obtained from silicon-containing compounds; it is not the same substance as silica.
details.first_principles: Doping modifies silicon's electrical properties.
details.does: Provides the semiconductor material used for devices such as transistors.
details.outcome: A useful electronic material that requires high purity for semiconductor applications.
details.useWhen: Making silicon-based semiconductor devices.

empowered_by.how: Produces material with controlled electrical properties.

verification.scope: Element identity, isolation milestone and semiconductor use.
verification.furtherResearch: Crystal growth, oxide-interface properties and specific fabrication processes.

details.definition: Semiconductor devices that control current. This mechanism example is a MOSFET, whose gate voltage controls conduction between source and drain.
details.motivation: Use an electrical control signal to permit or restrict another current path.
details.origin: Bell Labs demonstrated point-contact transistor action in December 1947. That historical device was not a MOSFET; the mechanism below describes the later field-effect family.
details.first_principles: An insulated gate creates an electric field that changes conduction in a semiconductor channel.
details.does: Changing gate voltage changes whether the channel provides a conducting path.
details.outcome: An electrically controlled switch; the switching abstraction depends on the device's actual voltage and conduction characteristics.
details.useWhen: A MOSFET implementation needs voltage-controlled switching.

empowered_by.how: The insulated gate's field controls channel conduction.

verification.scope: Introductory MOSFET mechanism plus a distinct early transistor milestone.

claims.agreement: Bell Labs history and Brattain's dated laboratory record corroborate the December 1947 point-contact milestone.

verification.furtherResearch: MOSFET invention history, BJT operation, leakage, capacitance, switching energy and device-specific limits.

details.definition: A diode is a two-terminal device with asymmetric current-voltage behavior; this example uses a p-n junction.
details.motivation: Favor conduction in one direction for rectification.
details.origin: Mechanism lineage: joining p-type and n-type semiconductor regions forms a junction. This does not date the invention of every diode family.
details.first_principles: Forward and reverse bias change the junction barrier and its conduction.
details.does: Conducts substantially under suitable forward bias; reverse current is small before breakdown, not identically zero.
details.outcome: Directional conduction with forward voltage drop and reverse-voltage limits.
details.useWhen: Rectifying current with a diode selected for the required current and voltage.

empowered_by.how: Differently doped regions produce bias-dependent conduction.

verification.scope: Basic p-n rectifying diode behavior; no historical priority claim.
verification.furtherResearch: Schottky, Zener, LED and photodiode mechanisms; recovery, capacitance and thermal limits.

details.definition: An integrated circuit combines electronic circuit elements on semiconductor material.
details.motivation: Build interconnected circuits in a compact manufactured form.
details.origin: Jack Kilby demonstrated a working integrated circuit at Texas Instruments on September 12, 1958. This milestone does not attribute all subsequent fabrication advances to him.
details.first_principles: Circuit function comes from both devices and their interconnections.
details.does: Fabrication forms device regions and conducting interconnects on a die.
details.outcome: Compact electronic circuits that require manufacturing, testing and packaging.
details.useWhen: Implementing electronic functions in a semiconductor chip.

empowered_by.how: Patterns devices and interconnects into the chip.

verification.scope: Basic IC construction and Kilby's documented demonstration.
verification.furtherResearch: Noyce's planar integration, analog versus digital ICs, process economics and packaging variants.

details.definition: Semiconductor fabrication builds patterned devices and interconnections on a wafer.
details.motivation: Manufacture many connected circuit elements at small dimensions.
details.origin: Process lineage: prepared silicon wafers undergo repeated patterning and material-processing steps. The sources describe manufacturing, not the first invention of VLSI.
details.first_principles: Lithography defines a pattern; deposition, etching and doping change selected regions of material.
details.does: Repeats processing across layers, forms interconnects, tests dies, then separates and packages them.
details.outcome: Physical chips; manufacturing needs repeated precision steps and testing for defects.
details.useWhen: Producing integrated semiconductor circuits from a design.

empowered_by.how: Serves as the substrate on which device regions and interconnect layers are formed.
empowered_by.forCase: The silicon manufacturing flows illustrated by Intel and ASML.

verification.scope: Introductory silicon chip manufacturing; no node-size or universal process recipe claim.
verification.furtherResearch: VLSI design methodology, process integration, yield and technology-specific constraints. Intel's illustrated process is explicitly a 45 nm-era example.

lectures.title: Intel: From Sand to Silicon
lectures.role: Manufacturer's explanatory video, not a university lecture.

edges.label: Uses language-defined execution and synchronization semantics
details: Concurrency memory models constrain what shared-memory reads may observe.
Language-defined synchronization contributes ordering between actions; address isolation does not supply this contract.
Sources: https://go.dev/ref/mem ; https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-17.html#jls-17.4

edges.label: Uses cached address translations
details: A TLB caches translations; page tables provide the mappings on a miss.
A translation-cache miss need not be a page fault.
Sources: https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf ; https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.1810/2023/xv6/book-riscv-rev3.pdf#page=31

edges.label: Uses messaging with explicit failure handling
details: Raft handles delayed, lost and reordered messages; safety does not require every message to arrive.
Transport cannot by itself establish replicated-log agreement. Progress depends on a communicating majority and suitable timing.
Sources: https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf sections 2 and 5 ; https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/labs/lab-raft1.html
This transport edge describes a possible implementation; Raft does not require TCP specifically.

edges.label: Uses B-tree indexes in applicable access paths
details: An ordered index can accelerate matching lookups; database engines also execute table scans.
B-trees are an implementation choice, not a requirement of the relational model.
Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html ; https://www.sqlite.org/queryplanner.html

edges.label: Uses HTTP/TLS for HTTPS APIs
details: For HTTPS APIs, HTTP defines request/response semantics and TLS protects the connection.
This is a conditional dependency for HTTPS, not a claim that every API uses HTTP.
Sources: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html section 4.2.2 ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.html section 1

edges.label: Maps resident pages to physical memory
details: For paged virtual memory, resident virtual pages map to physical frames. Source evidence is recorded in os_virtual_memory.details.verification.

edges.label: Uses DRAM storage cells
details: For DRAM main memory, arrays of dynamic cells hold data and require refresh. Source evidence is recorded in architecture_main_memory.details.verification.

edges.label: Uses an access transistor in a DRAM cell
details: The one-transistor DRAM design uses a transistor to access capacitor storage. Source evidence is recorded in logic_memory_circuits.details.verification.

edges.label: Uses transistor switching in CMOS
details: Conditional on CMOS implementation. Source evidence is recorded in logic_logic_gates.details.verification.

edges.label: Interconnects gates to compute a function
details: For gate-based combinational design. Source evidence is recorded in logic_combinational_circuits.details.verification.

edges.label: Computes the next state
details: For the synchronous construction described in the entry. Source evidence is recorded in logic_sequential_circuits.details.verification.

edges.label: Retains state in clocked storage
details: For edge-triggered synchronous construction. Source evidence is recorded in logic_sequential_circuits.details.verification.

edges.label: Uses controlled feedback in latches
details: For the master/slave D construction. Source evidence is recorded in logic_flip-flops.details.verification.

edges.label: Stores count bits
details: For synchronous binary counters. Source evidence is recorded in logic_counters.details.verification.

edges.label: Uses arithmetic and selection logic
details: For the teaching ALU implementations described in the entry. Source evidence is recorded in logic_adders___alus.details.verification.

edges.label: Realizes transitions with logic and stored state
details: Applies to clocked hardware realization, not to the abstract definition of an FSM. Source evidence is recorded in logic_finite-state_machines.details.verification.

edges.label: Models data as relations over domains
details: The formal model defines relations as sets of tuples over domains.
This is a conceptual dependency; SQL implementations differ from the pure mathematical model.
Sources: https://doi.org/10.1145/362384.362685 ; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/7.0/sql26902.htm

edges.label: Expresses operations over relational tables
details: SQL's relational core describes queries and changes over tables while the DBMS chooses execution procedures.
SQL contains features and semantics beyond pure relational algebra.
Sources: https://research.ibm.com/publications/sequel-a-struciured-english-query-language ; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html

edges.label: Uses SQL in the relational branch
details: SQL database applications use the language to define, query, and modify relational data.
This edge is conditional: non-SQL and non-relational databases exist.
Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html ; https://sqlite.org/lang.html

edges.label: Coordinates concurrent access and recovery
details: Representative transaction systems use concurrency control to manage visibility and conflicts, plus logging and recovery for commit guarantees.
Exact locking, MVCC, logging, and recovery algorithms vary by DBMS.
Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc.html ; https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-830-database-systems-fall-2010/10b223dc3daf6fda4001272799b153a0_MIT6_830F10_lec10.pdf
